title: Uncertainty in derived quantities

learning_outcomes.text: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

prior_knowledge_summary: Precision is judged from agreement among repeated measurements, indicated by their spread or range.
Accuracy is judged by closeness to the true value.
Instrument resolution is the smallest change that an instrument can distinguish.
Students can convert prefixes and derived units and check unit consistency.
new_learning: Absolute uncertainty has the same unit as the measured quantity.
Fractional uncertainty is absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, and percentage uncertainty is the fractional uncertainty multiplied by 100 percent.
For sums and differences, absolute uncertainties are added.
For products and quotients, fractional or percentage uncertainties are added.
For a quantity raised to a power, its fractional or percentage uncertainty is multiplied by the magnitude of that power.
not_yet_taught: Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

visual_planning.reason: Six figures separate uncertainty forms, show the two combination rules, expose the subtracting-uncertainties misconception, model powers and finish with a complete propagation route.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: A small uncertainty can grow
content: A square tile has side length (10.0 ± 0.2) cm. The side is uncertain by only 2 percent. Is its area also uncertain by only 2 percent?
The area uses the same uncertain length twice: A = l × l. Both factors can move the result, so the area uncertainty is 4 percent, not 2 percent.
A derived quantity combines measurements. We therefore need rules that follow the mathematical operation instead of guessing from the size of one uncertainty.

figure.purpose: Create the need for propagation by showing one uncertain length appearing twice in an area
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a square labelled l on two perpendicular sides, with l = (10.0 ± 0.2) cm. Beside it show two coloured uncertainty contribution arrows entering A = l × l. Ask '2 percent or 4 percent?' without revealing the answer.
figure.alt_text: An uncertain side length appears twice in the expression for the area of a square.

blocks.title: Three ways to state one uncertainty
content: For x = (8.00 ± 0.12) cm, 0.12 cm is the absolute uncertainty. It has the same unit as x.
The fractional uncertainty is Δx / x = 0.12 / 8.00 = 0.015. It has no unit.
The percentage uncertainty is (Δx / x) × 100 percent = 1.5 percent. It also has no unit.
These are not three different errors. They are three forms of the same uncertainty. To return from a fraction to an absolute uncertainty, use Δx = fractional uncertainty × x.
Independent check: 1.5 percent of 8.00 cm is 0.120 cm, so the conversion returns the original absolute uncertainty.

figure.purpose: Link absolute, fractional and percentage forms without treating them as separate quantities
figure.brief: Create a colourful hand-drawn triangular conversion map. Place 0.12 cm at the absolute corner, 0.015 at the fractional corner and 1.5 percent at the percentage corner. Label arrows divide by measured value, multiply by measured value, multiply by 100 and divide by 100.
figure.alt_text: A conversion map connects absolute uncertainty, fractional uncertainty and percentage uncertainty.

blocks.title: For addition or subtraction, add absolute uncertainties
content: A length is found by subtracting two scale readings: L = x - y. The readings are x = (42.6 ± 0.3) mm and y = (18.2 ± 0.2) mm.
The central value is L = 42.6 mm - 18.2 mm = 24.4 mm.
For a sum or difference, add absolute uncertainties: ΔL = 0.3 mm + 0.2 mm = 0.5 mm. Therefore L = (24.4 ± 0.5) mm.
Subtraction in the equation does not mean subtracting uncertainties. One reading may be high while the other is low, making their difference move by both absolute amounts.
Independent check with extremes: the largest possible difference is 42.9 mm - 18.0 mm = 24.9 mm, which is 0.5 mm above the central value.

figure.purpose: Show why absolute uncertainty contributions add even when measured values are subtracted
figure.brief: Draw two short number-line intervals for x and y, then a third interval for L = x - y. Highlight the extreme pair x high and y low, carrying +0.3 mm and +0.2 mm into a total ±0.5 mm. Keep the central subtraction visible.
figure.alt_text: Extreme scale readings show two absolute uncertainty contributions widening a difference by 0.5 millimetres.

blocks.title: For multiplication or division, add fractional uncertainties
content: A rectangular card has l = (8.40 ± 0.05) cm and w = (3.20 ± 0.03) cm. Its area is A = lw = 8.40 × 3.20 = 26.88 cm².
The percentage contribution from l is (0.05 / 8.40) × 100 percent = 0.595 percent. The contribution from w is (0.03 / 3.20) × 100 percent = 0.938 percent.
For a product, add percentage uncertainties: percentage uncertainty in A = 0.595 percent + 0.938 percent = 1.53 percent.
The absolute uncertainty is ΔA = 0.0153 × 26.88 cm² = 0.412 cm², which rounds to 0.4 cm². Quote A = (26.9 ± 0.4) cm².
The same addition rule applies to a quotient because relative changes in either the numerator or denominator change the result.

figure.purpose: Model a full product propagation from absolute inputs to a final absolute uncertainty
figure.brief: Create a rectangular four-stage teacher sketch: measured l and w, two percentage conversion cards, a plus sign joining 0.595 percent and 0.938 percent, then a final area card (26.9 ± 0.4) cm squared. Use distinct colours for the two measurement contributions.
figure.alt_text: Two length uncertainties are converted to percentages, added and converted to an absolute area uncertainty.

blocks.title: A power repeats an uncertainty contribution
content: If y is proportional to x to the power n, the percentage uncertainty in y contributed by x is the magnitude of n times the percentage uncertainty in x.

For A = πr², an exact constant such as π adds no measurement uncertainty. If r = (2.50 ± 0.02) cm, the percentage uncertainty in r is 0.8 percent, so the percentage uncertainty in A is 2 × 0.8 percent = 1.6 percent.
The central area is π(2.50 cm)² = 19.635 cm². Its absolute uncertainty is 0.016 × 19.635 cm² = 0.314 cm², so A = (19.6 ± 0.3) cm².

A denominator power still contributes positively. For y = a / b², add the percentage uncertainty in a to twice the percentage uncertainty in b. The minus sign in the exponent changes how the value responds, not the size of the uncertainty contribution.

figure.purpose: Make an exponent visible as the number of repeated relative uncertainty contributions
figure.brief: Draw a colourful exponent flow diagram. Show r squared splitting into two identical 0.8 percent contribution tiles that combine to 1.6 percent. Beside it show b to the power minus two also producing two positive contribution tiles. Mark π as exact with zero contribution.
figure.alt_text: A squared measurement produces two equal percentage uncertainty contributions whether it is in a numerator or denominator.

blocks.title: Do not add unlike forms
content: It can feel efficient to add every number beside a plus-or-minus sign. That fails when the uncertainties have different units or when the equation uses multiplication.
For a product, convert every input uncertainty to the same fractional or percentage form before adding. For a sum or difference, keep every input uncertainty in the same absolute unit before adding.
For example, 0.02 m cannot be added directly to 3 percent. Convert 0.02 m using its measured value, or convert 3 percent back to an absolute uncertainty, according to the operation being propagated.
Exact numbers such as 2, π or a stated exact conversion factor do not receive an uncertainty contribution.

figure.purpose: Prevent addition of incompatible uncertainty forms and select the rule from the operation
figure.brief: Create a hand-drawn two-lane decision route. Lane one: plus or minus values leads to same-unit absolute uncertainties. Lane two: multiply, divide or powers leads to fractional or percentage uncertainties. Put 0.02 m plus 3 percent behind a red stop symbol until both are converted to the same form.
figure.alt_text: A decision route separates absolute uncertainty rules from fractional and percentage uncertainty rules.

blocks.title: Carry one result through a complete propagation
content: A supplied relation is R = kL³ / t², where k is exact. Measurements are L = (4.80 ± 0.06) cm and t = (2.40 ± 0.03) ms. When SI units are used, R is in watts.
First use earlier unit work: L = 0.0480 m and t = 0.00240 s. Then R = 0.0200 × (0.0480)³ / (0.00240)² = 0.384 W.
Both input percentage uncertainties are 1.25 percent. The L³ contribution is 3 × 1.25 percent = 3.75 percent. The t² contribution is 2 × 1.25 percent = 2.50 percent.
Add the contributions: percentage uncertainty in R = 6.25 percent. Then ΔR = 0.0625 × 0.384 W = 0.0240 W.
The result is R = (0.384 ± 0.024) W. Independent check: 0.024 / 0.384 = 0.0625, which returns 6.25 percent.

blocks.title: Choose the rule from the operation
content: Start by calculating the central derived value with consistent units.
For addition or subtraction, add absolute uncertainties in a common unit.
For multiplication or division, add fractional or percentage uncertainties. Multiply a contribution by the magnitude of its power.
Convert the combined fractional or percentage uncertainty back to an absolute uncertainty when the final answer requires plus-or-minus form.
Round the uncertainty sensibly and quote the central value to the same decimal place. These rules assess uncertainty size only; scalar and vector ideas begin in the next lesson.
